blocks.p: Rei went back to the library in Itabashi, because Higuchi had starred the name twice. By now a starred name in that margin was the only kind of warning Rei had learned to obey.

It was the same trip as before, and it felt different the second time. The Saikyō line train was crowded at the end of the afternoon. Everyone was holding a phone or a fan, and the air conditioning lost the fight with the heat every time the doors opened. At Ikebukuro a wave of people poured off, and many of them carried bags of fruit and boxes of sweets wrapped in paper. They were travelling home for Obon, back to the towns where their families kept their graves. On the slow Tōbu Tōjō train out to Tokiwadai, an old man across the aisle held a bunch of white chrysanthemums upright on his knee the whole way, as carefully as if it were a candle.

Watanabe Jun was at the returns cart in the same cardigan two sizes too big. From the periodicals corner Rei watched him work for most of an hour. The wrongness around him was worse than the first time. It was never dramatic. It was just a deepening of that half-step of dimness. The air near him now had the faded colour of an old photograph left too long in a drawer.

He shelved a stack of children's picture books. His hand shook on the last one. He stood very still until the shaking stopped, the way a man stands still when standing is the only thing he has left the strength to do. Rei understood that he was not watching a holder hold. He was watching a holder lose his grip, one finger at a time, and decide each time not to tell anyone.
As the library emptied toward closing, Rei did what he had come to do. He let Watanabe see that he was watching.

Watanabe did not jump. He set the last book down and looked at Rei with the tired recognition of a man who has waited years for someone to notice. The relief on his face was so open it was hard to look at. On a face that gentle, relief was a confession. He had been alone with this since before Rei could read.

"You can tell," he said. It was not a question. His voice was dimmed too, soft at the edges. It was the voice of someone who had spent himself on something invisible for so long that he had forgotten how to be loud. "Most people just feel cold near me and move their chair. You're the first one in a long time who looked at where the cold was coming from."

He made tea in the staff room with a kettle that took too long. In a flat, unhurried voice, the way people talk about the weather, he told Rei what he was. The sixth of the Thirteen. He carried Despair the way a stone wall holds back a hillside. And lately the hillside had been getting heavier.

"I've tried to retire three times," he said. "There's no way to do it. Nobody built one. The seat just stays where you are." He almost smiled. "I find that very accurate, as a description of despair."
"Gin wrote that you say despair sees more clearly than anything else."
"Despair handled properly is the emotion that sees reality most accurately. That's what I say." He shrugged. "It's either wisdom or a symptom. It's both."
He wrapped both hands round his cup to take the warmth he could no longer quite make for himself.

"It used to be that I held it and it held still. Now I hold it and it leans. North. Always north now. Toward the empty place." He was quiet for a moment. "And there's something else. Every seat has a shadow on the other side. A thing made of the same feeling, at its worst. Most of them we've never seen. Mine has a name now. Kishin. It's in Takinogawa, wearing a woman like a coat, and it is eating my chair from under me. The empty seat pulls. Kishin bites." He looked down at the tea. "We can kill things like that, you know. Holders. It's the one thing they're afraid of. And they can ride us. That's the one thing we're afraid of."
Then he asked the question that turned a starred name into a person Rei could ruin or save.
"I don't suppose you came here to help. People don't, usually. But I find I'd very much like it if you had."
He let Rei follow him for a day. The day was the horror, because nothing happened in it that anyone else could have seen.

Watanabe woke at five in a one-room flat a few streets from the library. The first thing he did, before the light and before tea, was something he called the settling. He sat on the edge of his futon and reached out, inside himself and across his whole district, looking for its despair. All of it. The man on the night shift who had stopped opening his post. The widow three floors down who had started giving her things away. The boy who studied the train timetables, and not because he wanted to ride the trains. Watanabe gathered it the way a person gathers spilled rice off a floor, grain by grain, into himself, so that none of them had to carry the full killing weight of it alone.

"That's the seat," he said, watching Rei's face. "Not a throne. A drain. The feeling runs through the district, and a holder is the place it runs to. Keep it moving, keep it passing through you, and it never sits still long enough to pool. When it pools, that's where suffering beings come from. Grief or despair left lying in one place until it thickens into something with a want of its own. My job is to make sure there's never enough lying still for that."

Rei spent the morning learning that a holder's mercy is invisible on purpose. Nobody in this ward walked into the river in August, and the reason was a slight man in a cardigan who got up before dawn. He took the weight of their worst hour into a body that was not built to store it. He had done it every single morning for longer than he would say. No one knew. That was the point.
"If they knew, they'd thank me," he said. "Then they'd feel they owed me. And the owing is its own despair. So I make sure they never find out. A seat held right is a seat no one can see."

He said it without bitterness. That was the part that got under Rei's skin. A man with no bitterness about giving up his whole life for no thanks is a man who has used up his bitterness too, along with everything else.
Then, in the middle of a sentence, the leaning took him.

Rei saw it happen. The dimness around Watanabe deepened, fast, toward the north. Rei felt the pull in his own teeth, like a held musical note sliding a half-step lower. Watanabe grabbed the edge of the table and held on until his knuckles went white. He breathed in a slow, careful, counted way, like a man holding up a wall with nothing but his attention.
It passed. He let go of the table.

"That's new," he said, and tried to smile. "This year. The empty chair pulling on the full ones. Some mornings the settling takes everything I've got and there's nothing left for... you know. Lunch. Standing up. Wanting to."

He looked at the window that faced north, toward Kita, toward the wound. For one second the gentleness slipped, and Rei saw what was under it. A man being slowly poured out through a hole he had not made and could not plug.
It was not Watanabe who let go first.

The news reached him the way news travels among the Thirteen. Gin's notes said their network had no name and no schedule. It worked by recognition, the way two people carrying the same heavy load can pick each other out across a crowded platform. Watanabe was a telepath. That evening, as the library was closing, he went still over the returns cart and said, very quietly, "Oh." It was the way people say it when the phone rings at the wrong hour.

"The fourth," he said. "Nakashima Yuna. She carries Fear. She's gone to the place a holder goes when the weight gets heavier than the will." He was already reaching for his coat. "Mori-san will have felt it too. He'll be awake at his boiler, holding on to the rest of us the way he always does. He's the eldest. When something like this happens we all look to him first." He stopped in the doorway. "I'm going to her. You can come if you can keep your feet."

They went north together, into the part of the city where the veil was thin. Watanabe said almost nothing in the taxi. He sat with his eyes shut and his hands flat on his knees, listening to something Rei could not hear, and now and then he told the driver to turn. The driver had a little paper lantern hanging from his mirror for Obon, and it swung at every corner. By the time they found the right building, it was the hour before dawn. It was a danchi in Kita. In a small room with a single bed lay a woman who was not dying. Dying would have been ordinary. She was letting go. Her seat was coming open while they watched, and years of held Fear were coming loose all at once.

Rei had stood in thin places before. He had walked lanes that folded back on themselves. He had read his brother's traces in the membrane, the skin between this world and the other side. He had felt the far shore breathing through a torn seam. None of it had prepared him for the sound a register makes when it lets go.

It was not a sound. It was a lurch. The whole membrane over Kita gave one sick shudder, like a ferry hitting the wake of a ship no one can see. For three full seconds, every frightened thing Yuna had been holding back from the northern wards arrived in the people living there, all at once.

Rei felt it as a wave of pure terror with no reason behind it. It had nothing to do with him, and it went through him anyway. He watched Watanabe brace himself against the doorframe and take what he could of it. Not all of it. He did not have the strength for all of it. But he took a share, by instinct, the way a driver throws an arm across the passenger in a crash.
And Rei understood what the Thirteen were. Not rulers. Catchers. Twelve pairs of arms thrown across a city at the moment it brakes too hard.

When it settled, Yuna was asleep. Simply, ordinarily asleep, a tired woman who had held something terrible for years and had finally set it down. Her seat stood empty for now. The fourth chair had been pulled out from the table, and Rei could feel the table tilt further toward the gap because of it.
Watanabe slid down the doorframe and sat on the floor, grey and empty.

"Two empty chairs now," he said. "Hers, until she can climb back into it, and the thirteenth. The leaning will get worse for the rest of us. For me. Every chair that opens pulls harder on the ones still full."
"What happens if she can't climb back?"

"Then the succession reaches for someone else. The CVD keeps a list it doesn't show anyone. People they rank Singularity. Secret candidates for the Thirteen, in case one of us falls. Most of them have no idea that's what they're for." He looked up at Rei from the floor. "I'm next, you understand. Nearest the wound, weakest of the lot. I've about a season left in me. Less, if another one goes. That's not me being sad. I stopped being sad years ago. That's just the arithmetic, and I thought you'd want it straight."

Rei walked Watanabe home from the danchi as the sky turned the colour of dishwater. Neither of them wanted a train. They followed the Shakujii River upstream toward Itabashi. It is a narrow river that runs through a deep concrete channel, with cherry trees leaning over its walls. At that hour the water was black and slow. A man in a vest was already out walking a small white dog. Delivery bikes clattered over the little bridges. On the way they passed a small memorial on the bank, where someone had set out fresh flowers, a cup of sake and a single paper lantern that had not yet been lit.

blocks.cap: Okuma Sumi at the riverside memorial, and the grief that gathers there
Okuma Sumi, who tends the riverside memorial

blocks.p: An old woman knelt there, changing the water in a jar. She was well into her seventies, in a faded summer kimono with the sleeves tied back. She moved slowly and with great care, the way people move in a place they have visited every day for years.
She looked up as they passed. Her eyes went straight past Rei and settled on Watanabe.
"It's you," she said. "I thought so. Some evenings the water goes very quiet, and very heavy, and then it lifts again. As if somebody upstream had taken a sack off its back. I always wondered who."
Watanabe stopped. For a moment Rei thought he would deny it. Instead he bowed, quite deeply.
"Okuma-san," he said. "I didn't know you'd noticed."

"Grief gathers at the water like silt," the old woman said. "I tend it. Some nights, something answers back." She set the jar down. "This summer it answers more than it should. You look very tired, young man."
"I am," Watanabe said simply.

She nodded as if that settled something, and turned back to her flowers. As they walked on, Rei looked back once. She was speaking softly to the river, the way people speak to someone who has just gone into the next room.

"She lost someone to that river a long time ago," Watanabe said quietly. "She's been coming every evening since. It isn't healthy, what she's built there. But it isn't mine to take from her either." He was silent for a few steps. "That's most of the job. Knowing what isn't yours to take."
In the grey week that followed, Rei made a decision. He would give Watanabe Jun one morning off.

He walked to Itabashi along the river in the dark, before five, while the streetlights were still on and the first crows were starting up. He sat on the edge of Watanabe's futon and told him to stay lying down. When the hour came, Rei did the settling himself. Rei had two registers, two kinds of feeling the veil could move through him, and he had spent his whole life pressing them down. Now he opened them on purpose. He reached out into the district and found the despair of strangers, grain by grain. The man who had stopped opening his post. The widow giving her things away. The boy with the timetables. He gathered it.

It was the worst thing he had ever done on purpose. He did not stop. A few steps away Watanabe was breathing the slow, even breath of a man resting for the first time in a year. The resting was the whole point. Rei had come to be the place the weight could run to, so that just this once, Watanabe would not have to be.

It came into him, and it did not feel like sadness. That was the lie the word despair told. It felt like gravity. A steady, true, downward pull. The simple physical fact that down exists and everything falls toward it. Holding it meant standing inside that fact and choosing, with his whole body, to stay upright, for people who would never know there had been a choice.

For one morning, Rei felt what Watanabe felt every morning. What Yuna had felt for years before her arms gave out. What the seat really cost the person in it. It was not a wound that someone does to a holder. It was an agreement, made again at every dawn, to be broken a little, so that a whole ward could wake up and think it had simply found the strength to face the day.

By seven he was out in the streets of the district, on his knees on a stranger's stairwell. He understood the registry from the inside now. He understood why the Healer's offer looked like mercy. And he understood exactly how something that is mercy can also be the trap.

When he came back, Watanabe was up and had made the slow tea. He took one look at Rei's face and knew what Rei had done, and what it had taught him. For the first time since they met, his eyes were wet, and not for himself.

"Now you know," he said. "Now you know it isn't done to us. We say yes. Every morning, we say yes, and the saying is the seat. That's why a thing that wants a chair can't just take it. It has to get a living register to say yes in a body that fits. That's what it's doing to your brother, isn't it. Teaching a hand to say yes."

He set the tea in front of Rei and folded Rei's hands round the cup for the warmth, the way he warmed his own. Then he looked at Rei for a long time, the way the telepath in him looked at everything, and his face changed.
"Oh," he said softly. "You're the shape of the thirteenth."
Rei did not answer. He did not know how.
"Your brother copied the ledger, didn't he. Did he ever write down what the thirteenth actually is?"
"He wrote that the CVD files it as null-emotive. That he thought that was wrong, and couldn't say what was right."

Watanabe nodded slowly. "Their instruments measure feeling by how much it moves. Duty doesn't move. It holds. So the needle sits still and they write down nothing there. But it isn't empty. It's full. So full there's no room in it for anything else. It's what duty becomes when it's been the only thing for so long that there's no self left that remembers what came before it." He turned his cup. "That's why it's so hard to fill. The seat needs someone with many doors open at once. Someone deep enough to hold that one feeling that never changes, without letting it turn into grief or rage or any of the rest of ours. Most people would be swallowed. The ones it wants don't get swallowed. The old ones say the next holder of Duty doesn't become less himself. He just becomes the person who carries it, and his ordinary life goes on with that inside it."
"And the ones working against you?"

"They don't want to take the thirteenth. They want it never filled. A vacant thirteenth means the Axis is holding it alone, stretched too thin. And a thing stretched that thin makes mistakes. They've been living off its mistakes for three years." He pushed the tea an inch closer to Rei. "You shouldn't have learned any of this. But God help me, I'm glad someone finally did. I've been the only one who knew what it felt like for a very long time."
For the rest of August, Watanabe Jun stayed at the returns cart in his cardigan, holding. That was what the seat was. Nobody had given him a way out that did not cost a brother or a city.

Rei visited when he could. Each time, Watanabe was dimmer, the half-step of darkness deepening toward a whole one. The pull to the north got a little worse every time another chair so much as creaked. Each time he greeted Rei with the same open relief, the same slow tea and the same refusal to complain. And each time Rei carried away the lesson of the morning of the settling. The wall is held up by consent. A register says yes. The whole patient effort on the far side was a plan to win one yes, in one borrowed hand.

That knowledge followed him out of the library and into every room for the rest of the month. On the good nights it felt like a weapon. The chair needs a yes, he would tell himself on the train home, his face reflected in the dark window. So a yes held back is a chair left empty. And a brother who learns not to agree starves the whole plot at the root.

On the bad nights it felt like something else. He had been shaped to fit now. He had done the settling, and the seat remembered him. Lying awake, he caught himself thinking that the cleanest way to save the twelve and spare Gin might be to say yes himself, in a body that fit. Watanabe had shown him exactly how. He did not like how calm the thought was.
And under all of it was grief. A gentle, dimming man counting down his last season. It was the truest thing anyone had told him about what the wall costs the people who are the wall.
On the last good visit, Watanabe asked him not to be there when it happened.

"You've felt one go," he said. "You don't need to feel mine. Go and do the thing only you can do. You're the one with two of yourself and a hand the chair wants. You're the only piece on this board that isn't already spent."

He shelved the last picture book of the day. His hand did not shake this time. Rei could see what that steadiness cost him. He was holding his hand still for Rei's sake, so that the last picture Rei kept of him would be a steady one.

"Close the chair if you can do it without becoming me," he said. "And if you can't..." He stopped, and started again, dimmer. "If you can't, then become me knowing what it is. With your eyes open. The way I never got to choose it. That's the only mercy I've got to give you, and it's a poor one, and I'm sorry it's the truth."

On the train home that night, Rei thought back to where all of this had started. It was the night on the floor of the Crooked Shelf with the ledger open in front of him, when he had looked at the starred line with Watanabe's name on it and told Higuchi that he would go looking too. Now he had found the man, and he was losing him.
